body.head: At Walt Whitman’s Deathbed: The 1891-92 Leaves of Grass

div.p: Like many of Walt Whitman’s readers, my introduction to Leaves of Grass was the “Deathbed Edition.” Though my high school literature anthology contained only two of his poems, I sensed in Whitman something kindred and purchased the least expensive edition I could find: the Signet Classics paperback that promised me “the content and grouping of poems authorized by the poet for the final and complete edition of his masterpiece.” Walking home from the bookshop, I started reading, logically, the first poem of the first grouping and pressed forward. And like many of Whitman’s readers, I quickly found the nearly four hundred poems of Leaves of Grass to be a complicated puzzle without much of a guide. Not having studied Whitman’s life, I keenly sensed my lack of context for each grouping—at some point I learned that Whitman called them “clusters”—though I was still able to sit in awe with individual poems and sequences that struck me. I’ll never forget that Signet Classics Leaves of Grass; it was the first book I ever owned that, thrillingly, disintegrated from overuse. I agreed with its blurb that Leaves of Grass was a “masterpiece,” and supplying the necessary context to understand it became a decades-long study of Whitman’s life and nineteenth-century America.

I do not think my experience of the Deathbed Edition was unusual. Readers often find it disorienting, even with the guidance of introductions by scholars, historians, or poets that many publishers provide. Those readers who persist with Whitman usually seek out his writing in more straightforward and focused packaging. The twelve-poem first edition of Leaves of Grass from 1855 enjoys a wide popularity and has even been read as an American scripture. Readers discerning in Whitman what I first sensed in my high school textbook revel in standalone printings of “Calamus” and “Live Oak, with Moss.” Those who admire the Civil War docupoetics of “Drum-Taps” and “Memories of President Lincoln” now often encounter them in reissues of the self-contained Drum-Taps and Sequel to Drum-Taps, rather than as clusters in Leaves of Grass. These are in addition to the numerous compilations of selected poems and excerpts available.

Biographer and historian Gary Schmidgall acknowledges this retreat from the tangled and unwieldy Deathbed Edition of Leaves of Grass and toward Whitman’s earlier and more manageable work. In his introduction to Walt Whitman: Selected Poems 1855-1892, Schmidgall speaks for generations of “distinguished readers” who “agree that this long period of revision and accretion amounted to a devolution rather than an evolution.” While Whitman published over one hundred new poems from 1881 to 1892, Schmidgall’s volume includes only thirty-three from this period, selecting those that break from the aging Whitman’s “chaotic, unedifying, and, truth to tell, occasionally tedious form” that, in Schmidgall’s estimation, tends toward the “unremarkable or bombastic.” In making this stylistic claim, too, Schmidgall captures the estimation of many readers who encounter Whitman’s Deathbed Edition and other late life work.

It is evident, however, that the late Whitman felt differently about his final edition of Leaves of Grass. On the evening of January 23, 1892, Horace Traubel brought copies from Whitman’s publisher, David McKay, bound in dark green cloth. Traubel records the poet turning the book over in his hands by candlelight, saying, “this, of course, is the edition I swear by,” and offering revisions for the wording stamped on the spine, insisting on “Complete 1892.” It should be unmistakable to readers, “not casually, but radically,” Whitman argued, that although “we have had editions and editions and editions, this is to be in “future the only authentic and perfect.” He liked even the book’s unwieldiness because he felt in its heft the weight of his life’s work: “What a book it makes now—how plump! And with a pretty touch, too, as made up in this shape.” Decades of growth brought Leaves of Grass into a buxom fullness far from its slim and lithe 1855 debut (see Table 1 for the contents of the 1855 Leaves of Grass and its relationship to the contents of the Deathbed Edition).

Though Whitman insisted that the spine be labeled “1892,” its title page bears the expanded date of “1891-’2” beneath the publisher’s information. Ever since the third edition of Leaves of Grass, with its hyphenated “1860-61” on the title page, Whitman liked hyphenated dates. Encountering these, one might assume that the first year is the work’s date of copyright and the second of its distribution, but there are other books with differing dates on the copyright and title pages that Whitman (and Whitman scholars) did not span, such as Passage to India and Two Rivulets. So when Whitman’s title pages include a span—as do Memoranda During the War and Specimen Days & Collect, and the 1881-82 edition of Leaves of Grass—it suggests a certain authorial calculation. Ed Folsom, for example, notes that the third edition’s dating ominously portends “the final year of unstable peace with the first year of actual war,” an augury that is reversed with the “1865-6” Sequel to Drum-Taps, “straddling the last year of war and the first year of reconstruction.” Although the fifth edition of Leaves of Grass was copyrighted and sold in 1870, it is dated 1871 and was expanded in 1872, and has been known colloquially as the “1871-72 edition” (and is so identified in the Whitman Encyclopedia). Ten years later, Whitman placed the spanned date of 1881-82 on the title page of the edition published by James Osgood, and 1891-’92 on the one from David McKay ten years after that. These three editions mark successive ten-year intervals, with the final span portending Whitman’s last full year of corporeality and the year his afterlife commenced.

Each edition is an episode in the growth of Leaves of Grass, yet Whitman wrote in a letter to Richard Maurice Bucke that “to me the 1892 ed’n supersedes them all by far” (duk.00962; despite the span on the title page, Whitman nearly always referred to this as the “‘92 Edition” in conversation and correspondence). And as letters arrived from friends and admirers who received this latest printing, Traubel dutifully read to Whitman from those who celebrated it as a crowning achievement. Later, when discussing a volume of Selected Poems published by Charles Webster, Whitman told Traubel, “I know of nothing more essential to our purposes than to have the world realize the approved volume—the ‘92 edition—as the only really complete and satisfactory presentation of our case.” While Whitman did not affix the adjective “deathbed” to this printing—as this introduction will consider after an outline of the 1892 edition’s contents—the adjectives he uses in conversation and correspondence are bold: complete, authentic, perfect, approved.

From its opening pages, the 1891-92 Leaves of Grass insists on its completeness, tucking “Copyrights &c.” behind the title page. Following a bibliographic list of every edition from 1855 onward and its annexes (the “copyrights”), Whitman included an initialled notice (the “&c.”) that commands his readers’ attention with the printer’s manicule:
☞As there are now several editions of L. of G., different texts and dates, I wish to say that I prefer and recommend this present one, complete, for future printing, if there should be any; a copy and fac-simile, indeed, of the text of these 438 pages. The subsequent adjusting interval which is so important to form’d and launch’d work, books especially, has pass’d; and waiting till fully after that, I have given (pages 423-438) my concluding words.
Reprints of the Deathbed Edition are inconsistent in their inclusion of “Copyrights &c.,” as they are also with their inclusion of the closing “Backward Glance” essay. The list of copyrights for Leaves of Grass calls attention to those “editions and editions and editions” that Whitman mentioned to Traubel. But even as he softens his authorial directive into a preference and recommendation, Whitman is clear that the “adjusting interval” from 1855 to 1892, during which he tinkered with the structure of Leaves of Grass, is over. He is like a prophet declaring the end of the dispensation; with this edition, the canon has closed and there will be no new revelation.
